issue_snapshot.title: False positive invalid-name (C0103) for module-level TypedDict instantiation, regression from PR #10673
issue_snapshot.body:
### Bug description

After #10672 was fixed by #10673, pylint now flags `invalid-name` (C0103) for *any* module-level
variable assigned an **instance** of a `TypedDict`-derived class — not just for the functional
`typing.TypedDict("Name", {...})` type-definition syntax that #10672 was actually about.

`_should_check_class_regex()` treats an assignment as class-like whenever the inferred value is
a `bases.Instance` whose MRO contains an ancestor named `"TypedDict"`:

```python
if isinstance(inferred_assign_type, bases.Instance) and {
    "EnumMeta",
    "TypedDict",
}.intersection(
    {ancestor.name for ancestor in cast(InferenceResult, inferred_assign_type).mro()}
):
    return True
```

This is correct for the functional-syntax case (`X = typing.TypedDict("X", {...})`), where `X`
really does define a new type and should follow `class-rgx`. But it also fires for the completely
unrelated case of instantiating an *already-defined* TypedDict subclass to produce an ordinary
value — which is not a type definition at all and shouldn't be checked against `class-rgx`.

In the type-definition case, astroid already infers the assigned value as a `nodes.ClassDef`,
which is caught by the *first* branch of `_should_check_class_regex` (`isinstance(inferred_assign_type, nodes.ClassDef)`).
The second branch (the `Instance`/MRO check added by #10673) is only ever needed for the `EnumMeta`
case, not for `TypedDict`, and adding `"TypedDict"` to that same branch overreaches into plain
value construction.

### Minimal reproducer

```python
from typing import TypedDict


class Foo(TypedDict):
    value: str


_DEFAULT_VALUE = Foo(value='0')
```

### Configuration

```ini

```

### Command used

```shell
pylint --disable=all --enable=invalid-name repro.py
```

### Pylint output

```python
************* Module repro
repro.py:8:0: C0103: Class name "_DEFAULT_VALUE" doesn't conform to PascalCase naming style (invalid-name)
```

### Expected behavior

No `invalid-name` warning — `_DEFAULT_VALUE` is an ordinary module-level constant holding a plain `dict`-like value (`Foo` is a `dict` at runtime), not a class or a type definition. It should be checked against `const-rgx`/`variable-rgx`, not `class-rgx`.

### Pylint version

```shell
pylint 4.0.6
astroid 4.0.4
Python 3.14.6
```

### OS / Environment

Fedora 44

### Additional dependencies

```python

```

issue_snapshot.title: BUG: read_csv(sep=None) raises TypeError instead of falling back to the python engine
issue_snapshot.body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import io
import pandas as pd

pd.read_csv(io.StringIO("a;b\n1;2\n"), sep=None)
```

### Issue Description

`sep=None` asks pandas to sniff the separator with `csv.Sniffer`, which only the python engine implements. Up to and including 2.2.3, passing `sep=None` without an explicit engine fell back to the python engine with a `ParserWarning`, and passing `engine="c"` explicitly raised a clear `ValueError`. Since 3.0.0 the fallback is gone, and the option reaches the C parser, which fails on an unhandled `None`:

```
  File "pandas/_libs/parsers.pyx", line 481, in pandas._libs.parsers.TextReader.__cinit__
    if len(delimiter) > 1:
TypeError: object of type 'NoneType' has no len()
```

Behavior on `io.StringIO("a;b\n1;2\n")`:

| | 2.2.3 | 3.0.0 – 3.0.5, main |
|---|---|---|
| `sep=None` (default engine) | falls back to python + `ParserWarning` | `TypeError` |
| `sep=None, engine="c"` | `ValueError: the 'c' engine does not support sep=None with delim_whitespace=False` | `TypeError` |
| `sep=None, engine="python"` | works | works |

The `engine="pyarrow"` case is separate but worth fixing alongside, because it fails silently rather than loudly — it ignores `sep=None` and parses each line as one column:

```python
>>> pd.read_csv(io.StringIO("a;b\n1;2\n"), sep=None, engine="pyarrow")
   a;b
0  1;2
```

The cause looks like GH-58668 (`CLN: Remove deprecated read_csv(delim_whitespace=)`, 0fc033618c7). `_clean_options` previously had:

```python
if sep is None and not delim_whitespace:
    fallback_reason = "sep=None with delim_whitespace=False"
    engine = "python"
```

When `delim_whitespace` was removed, the whole branch was deleted rather than reduced to `if sep is None:`. `_clean_options` still handles the other python-only separator cases (`len(sep) > 1`, non-encodeable `sep`), so `sep=None` is now the only one with no branch, and `engine` stays `"c"`.

This also means the documentation is currently wrong: the `sep` entry in the `read_csv`/`read_table` docstrings and in the IO user guide both still state that with `sep=None` "the Python parsing engine ... will be used", which no longer happens.

### Expected Behavior

`sep=None` with no explicit engine should fall back to the python engine and emit a `ParserWarning`, as in 2.2.3 and as the docstring describes:

```python
>>> pd.read_csv(io.StringIO("a;b\n1;2\n"), sep=None)
   a  b
0  1  2
```

`engine="c"` with `sep=None` should raise a `ValueError` naming the unsupported option, consistent with how `skipfooter` and regex separators are reported. `engine="pyarrow"` should raise rather than silently return a single column.

### Installed Versions

<details>

Reproduced on 3.0.0, 3.0.5, and main (`3.1.0.dev0+1481.g1d6b36eb8ff`); works as documented on 2.2.3.

</details>

issue_snapshot.title: False negatives when passing `subprocess` command as keyword argument
issue_snapshot.body:
### Summary

Various [`flake8-bandit`-derived rules](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/#flake8-bandit-s) are triggered when calling one of the `subprocess` functions with a non-literal value as the first argument, as this is considered untrusted input. However, passing the array of command tokens as a keyword argument, i.e. `args=[...]`, silences the violation!

```console
➜ ruff check --select=S603 - <<< 'subprocess.check_output([foo])'
All checks passed!
➜ ruff check --select=S603 - <<< 'import subprocess; foo = input(); subprocess.check_output([foo])'
S603 `subprocess` call: check for execution of untrusted input
 --> -:1:35
  |
1 | import subprocess; foo = input(); subprocess.check_output([foo])
  |                                   ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

Found 1 error.
```

This appears to be due to the use of `call.arguments.args.first()` in this file:
https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/blob/5b48a040974781ba90b47c8df628f8fd9b6c95dd/crates/ruff_linter/src/rules/flake8_bandit/rules/shell_injection.rs#L321-L327

### Version

ruff 0.16.2 (5b48a0409 2026-08-07)

issue_snapshot.title: Return type for methods covered by `_simple_escaping_wrapper` is wrong
issue_snapshot.body: Currently you are using `_simple_escaping_wrapper` to extend most of the existing string methods, which is absolutely fine (although the type annotation for the decorator could be better), but the way you are applying the decorator is problematic, since mypy will not be able to infer that the return type for these methods has changed. So whenever you use these methods the type will be downgraded to `str` from `Markup`. Luckily most of these methods you are unlikely to use on markup, but `replace` is one that I've wanted to use on several occasions and had to use `type:ignore` to fix the typing issues. ``` html = Markup('some link') reveal_type(html) # Markup -> OK still_html = html.replace('${url}', 'http://example.com') reveal_type(still_html) # str -> Not OK ``` The second `reveal_type` should still be `Markup`, since `_simple_escaping_wrapper` preserves markup-safety. The simple way to fix this would just be to explicitly write out each method explicitly, rather than the hacky loop using `locals`. It wouldn't even really be that much more verbose than it is right now, in many ways it would actually be more simple to just write: ``` __getitem__ = _simple_escaping_wrapper(str.__getitem__) capitalize = _simple_escaping_wrapper(str.capitalize) title = _simple_escaping_wrapper(str.title) lower = _simple_escaping_wrapper(str.lower) upper = _simple_escaping_wrapper(str.upper) replace = _simple_escaping_wrapper(str.replace) ljust = _simple_escaping_wrapper(str.ljust) rjust = _simple_escaping_wrapper(str.rjust) lstrip = _simple_escaping_wrapper(str.lstrip) rstrip = _simple_escaping_wrapper(str.rstrip) center = _simple_escaping_wrapper(str.center) strip = _simple_escaping_wrapper(str.strip) translate = _simple_escaping_wrapper(str.translate) expandtabs = _simple_escaping_wrapper(str.expandtabs) swapcase = _simple_escaping_wrapper(str.swapcase) zfill = _simple_escaping_wrapper(str.zfill) ``` Environment: - Python version: 3.10 - MarkupSafe version: 2.1.2

issue_snapshot.title: Markup.striptags: comments now get replaced with a space
issue_snapshot.body:
In 2.1.4, if `Markup.striptags` is called, the comment gets replaced by a space. In versions before that it's completely removed from the output.

Test case to reproduce:

```
import unittest

from markupsafe import Markup

class MarkupSafeTest(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_striptags(self):
        value = 'x <!-- comment -->'
        self.assertEqual(Markup(value).striptags(), 'x')


if __name__ == '__main__':
    unittest.main()
```

With markupsafe 2.1.4 it fails, with 2.1.3 - it passes.

I'm running with Python 3.11

The issue was originally found by running the `test_striptags` jinja test case with markupsafe 2.1.4:

https://github.com/pallets/jinja/blob/3fd91e4d11bdd131d8c12805177dbe74d85e7b82/tests/test_filters.py#L94
